toc.title: Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

html:
1Artifacts and Commitments (SF 4.6)

"Scrum's artifacts represent work or value. They are designed to maximize transparency of key information. Thus, everyone inspecting them has the same basis for adaptation."

"Each artifact contains a commitment to ensure it provides information that enhances transparency and focus against which progress can be measured."

Artifact Its commitment Covered in
Product Backlog The Product Goal This topic
Sprint Backlog The Sprint Goal Topic 11
Increment The Definition of Done Topic 12

"These commitments exist to reinforce empiricism and the Scrum values for the Scrum Team and their stakeholders."

Old wording

The 2017 Guide had the same three artifacts but no "commitments": the Definition of Done appeared under the Increment, and the Sprint Goal under Sprint Planning. Commitments are new in 2020. The 2017 Guide also had a section called "Artifact Transparency"; the 2020 Guide treats transparency under Scrum Theory and through the commitments.

Exam angle

three artifacts, three commitments, matched in pairs: Product Backlog → Product Goal; Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal; Increment → Definition of Done. A common trap swaps them.

2The Product Backlog (SF 4.1, SF 4.2)

"The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team."

2.1 Purpose and attributes (list at least three)

Attribute Meaning
Emergent It changes as the product, the market and the team's understanding change; it is never "finished"
Ordered Items are in a sequence set by the Product Owner
Single source of work Everything the Scrum Team works on comes from it
Owned by one person The Product Owner is accountable for its management, but may delegate the work
Transparent It is visible and understood by everyone (the Product Owner ensures it)
Contains the Product Goal The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog; the rest emerges to fulfil it
Refined continuously Items are broken down and detailed as needed
Sized by the Developers The people who will do the work size the items

2.2 Why the Product Backlog is emergent (SF 4.2) Beyond the Guide

The Guide uses the word "emergent" and the idea that the Product Backlog "emerges" to define what will fulfil the Product Goal. The reasons follow from Scrum's theory:

  • Work is complex: what is needed cannot be known in full at the start; knowledge comes from experience.
  • Every Sprint Review brings feedback and changes in the environment; the Product Backlog "may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities".
  • Learning during Sprints reveals new, changed or unnecessary items.
  • Items are detailed only when needed, so effort is not wasted on items that may never be built (lean thinking).
Old wording

The 2017 Guide said: "A Product Backlog is never complete", "the Product Backlog is dynamic; it constantly changes", it is "a living artifact" and "the single source of requirements". The 2020 Guide says emergent and the single source of work.

3Product Backlog Items (SF 4.3)

The Guide: refinement is "an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size. Attributes often vary with the domain of work."

Attribute Notes
Description What the item is, so everyone understands it (Guide)
Order Its position in the Product Backlog (Guide)
Size How big the item is, determined by the Developers (Guide)
Value Often added; it helps the Product Owner order Beyond the Guide
Acceptance or test description Often added to show completeness Beyond the Guide

Ready for selection: "Product Backlog items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event. They usually acquire this degree of transparency after refining activities."

Sizing: "The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing. The Product Owner may influence the Developers by helping them understand and select trade-offs."

Old wording

The 2017 Guide listed the attributes "description, order, estimate, and value", and said items "often include test descriptions". The 2020 Guide says "description, order, and size" and removed the word "estimate". The Guide does not mention user stories or story points: they are common formats and techniques, not required by Scrum.

4Product Backlog Refinement (SF 3.5, SF 3.6)

"Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items. This is an ongoing activity."

4.1 When and by whom

  • The Product Backlog "is refined as needed" during the Sprint, and the Scrum Team "may refine these items" in Sprint Planning.
  • The Guide does not make refinement an event and sets no time allocation and no required format. The Scrum Team decides how and when.
  • The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, including making it understood. The Developers size the items. Both collaborate.

4.2 Activities (list at least three) Beyond the Guide

Activity What it is
Break down (split) large items into smaller ones The Guide's own definition
Add detail Description, and often value and an idea of how to tell it is done
Size the items By the Developers
Order or reorder By the Product Owner, using what has been learned
Clarify with stakeholders and users Questions, examples, constraints, dependencies
Remove or update items that are no longer relevant Keeps the Product Backlog useful

4.3 Reasons (give at least two) Beyond the Guide

Reason Why
Shared understanding The Product Owner, Developers and stakeholders understand why an item has value and what it needs
Ready items for Planning Items that can be Done within one Sprint are ready for selection, so Planning is faster and more reliable
Better forecasts and confidence Smaller, clearer items increase understanding and confidence in what fits
Transparency The Product Backlog is visible and understood (the Product Owner's accountability)
Early discovery of risks and dependencies Problems appear before the Sprint, not in the middle of it
Adaptation New information changes the order of the work
Old wording

The 2017 Guide defined refinement as "adding detail, estimates, and order", and said "refinement usually consumes no more than 10% of the capacity of the Development Team". The 2020 Guide removed the word "estimate" and the 10% guideline. "Grooming" is an older name that the Guide no longer uses.

5The Product Goal

"The Product Goal describes a future state of the product which can serve as a target for the Scrum Team to plan against. The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define "what" will fulfill the Product Goal."

Fact Guide wording
Product "A vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, well-defined users or customers. A product could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract"
Long-term objective "The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team"
One at a time "They must fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next"
Who The Product Owner develops and explicitly communicates it
Link to Sprints Each Sprint Goal moves the team toward it; progress toward the Product Goal is discussed at the Sprint Review
Old wording

The Product Goal is new in 2020. The 2017 Guide had no Product Goal; teams used a "vision" or "goal" informally.

6The Three Artifacts Compared (SF 4.1)

Product Backlog Sprint Backlog Increment
Purpose The single source of work: what is needed to improve the product The Developers' plan for the Sprint A concrete, usable step toward the Product Goal
Commitment Product Goal Sprint Goal Definition of Done
Owner The Product Owner (accountable) The Developers The Scrum Team (entire team is accountable)
Attributes Emergent · ordered · single source of work · refined continuously Sprint Goal (why) + selected items (what) + plan (how) · real-time · updated daily Additive to prior Increments · thoroughly verified · usable · meets the Definition of Done
Lifetime As long as the product exists One Sprint Added to all prior Increments

7Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

  1. The Product Backlog is emergent and ordered. It is never complete and not fixed up front.
  2. Single source of work. Work not in the Product Backlog is not undertaken by the Scrum Team.
  3. The Product Owner orders it and remains accountable if work is delegated. Stakeholders convince; they do not order.
  4. The Developers size. The Product Owner helps with trade-offs.
  5. Refinement is an activity, not an event, ongoing, with no prescribed time or format.
  6. Ready for selection = can be Done within one Sprint. Large or vague items are refined first.
  7. Attributes vary with the domain. The Guide names description, order and size. User stories and story points are not required.
  8. One Product Goal at a time. The team fulfils or abandons it before taking the next. It lives in the Product Backlog.
  9. Match the commitments: Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done to Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment.
  10. Old wording "Estimate", "never complete", "grooming", the 10 percent of capacity guideline and "Development Team" are 2017 terms.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A manager asks for a complete, fully detailed Product Backlog before the first Sprint begins. What is the best response from the Scrum Master?

  • AExplain that the Product Backlog is emergent: it starts with what is known and changes as learning grows
  • BAsk the Developers to write the complete Product Backlog, since they will build everything that is in it
  • CAgree and delay the first Sprint until every item has been described and approved by the stakeholders and the Scrum Master
  • DReplace it with a fixed requirements document that the stakeholders sign before the work begins
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. It evolves with learning and feedback, and items are detailed as needed. Waiting for completeness delays learning and conflicts with empiricism.

S2Stakeholders insist that every item in the Product Backlog must be fully detailed and sized now. What is the best answer?

  • ARefinement is ongoing: items are detailed as needed, and items that can be Done in one Sprint are ready
  • BAgree: all items must be refined equally, so that none of them surprises the Developers later, even if it is far down the list
  • COnly the Product Owner may refine items, because the Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog
  • DRefinement happens only in a two-day workshop before the first Sprint of each quarter
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Guide describes refinement as an ongoing activity of breaking down and further defining items. Items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection; there is no need to detail everything at once, which would be waste and would be overtaken by change.

S3A committee of stakeholders votes on the order of the Product Backlog each month. What should the Scrum Master advise?

  • AThis is the correct approach, since the stakeholders know the market and the Product Owner only records their vote
  • BThe Scrum Master should chair the vote and count the stakeholders' votes before the order is final
  • CThe Developers should chair the vote, because they will build the items in the order that is chosen
  • DThe Product Owner orders the Product Backlog; stakeholders make their case to the Product Owner
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Product Owner is one person, accountable for ordering the Product Backlog. Those wanting to change it do so by convincing the Product Owner.

S4How many Product Goals does a Scrum Team work on at a time, and where is the Product Goal?

  • ASeveral, in a separate document
  • BOne at a time, in the Product Backlog; the team fulfils or abandons it before taking the next
  • COne for each Developer
  • DNone: the Product Goal is the Sprint Goal
Show the answer

Answer: B. The Product Goal is the long-term objective of the Scrum Team and is in the Product Backlog. The Scrum Team must fulfil (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next.

S5The Developers do all refinement in a single session on the day before each Sprint and never during the Sprint. What does the Guide say?

  • AThis is required by Scrum: refinement is a single session held on the day before each Sprint begins
  • BRefinement must happen only in Sprint Planning, where the whole Scrum Team is present and can discuss items
  • CRefinement is an ongoing activity, and the Product Backlog is refined as needed, also during the Sprint
  • DRefinement is forbidden during the Sprint, because the Developers must not be disturbed while they work
Show the answer

Answer: C. During the Sprint the Product Backlog is refined as needed, and the Scrum Team may also refine items in Sprint Planning. The Guide neither prescribes a refinement session nor limits when it happens.

S6A team says that Scrum requires every Product Backlog item to be a user story sized in story points. What is the right answer?

  • AThe Guide does not require user stories or story points; attributes such as description, order and size vary
  • BThe Guide requires user stories, because they are the only format that describes the value of an item for the user of the product
  • CThe Guide requires story points, because they are the only way to size items without using hours
  • DThe Scrum Master decides the format of all items, so that every item in the Product Backlog looks alike
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Guide names description, order and size as examples of details added in refinement and says the attributes vary with the domain. Neither user stories nor story points are mentioned.

S7Sprint Planning takes too long because items are unclear and too large. Which practice would help most?

  • AAdd a second Sprint Planning
  • BStop selecting items
  • CAsk the stakeholders to select the items
  • DRefine the Product Backlog regularly, so that items are small, clear and ready for selection
Show the answer

Answer: D. Refinement breaks items into smaller and more precise ones, which makes them ready for selection and increases understanding and confidence in Planning.

S8Where is the commitment of the Product Backlog, and what is it?

  • AThe Sprint Goal, in the Sprint Backlog
  • BThe Product Goal, in the Product Backlog
  • CThe Definition of Done, in the Increment
  • DThe Product Owner's vision, outside the Product Backlog
Show the answer

Answer: B. Each artifact contains a commitment: for the Product Backlog it is the Product Goal, for the Sprint Backlog the Sprint Goal and for the Increment the Definition of Done.

S9In the middle of a Sprint, a new regulation creates an urgent item. What is the correct way to handle it?

  • AThe stakeholder adds it to the Sprint Backlog, because an urgent legal item overrides the planning of the Sprint and the work of the Developers
  • BThe Developers drop an item at random and take the new one, since they know best what fits in the Sprint
  • CThe Product Owner orders it in the Product Backlog and negotiates with the Developers whether it enters the Sprint
  • DThe Scrum Master cancels the Sprint, as a new regulation always makes the current Sprint Goal obsolete
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Product Backlog is the single source of work and the Product Owner orders it. Scope within the Sprint can be renegotiated between the Developers and the Product Owner, without endangering the Sprint Goal. Cancelling is only for an obsolete Sprint Goal.

S10Which pairs are correct?

  • AProduct Backlog and Definition of Done
  • BSprint Backlog and Product Goal
  • CIncrement and Sprint Goal
  • DProduct Backlog and Product Goal; Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal; Increment and Definition of Done
Show the answer

Answer: D. Each artifact has one commitment: the Product Backlog has the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog the Sprint Goal and the Increment the Definition of Done.

8.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is the Product Backlog?

Show the answer

An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product; the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.

R2Who is accountable for the Product Backlog?

Show the answer

The Product Owner.

R3Name at least three attributes of the Product Backlog.

Show the answer

Emergent; ordered; the single source of work; owned by the Product Owner; transparent; contains the Product Goal; refined continuously.

R4Why is the Product Backlog emergent?

Show the answer

The work is complex and the product, market and understanding change; Reviews and learning change what is needed; items are detailed only when needed.

R5What are Product Backlog items' attributes in the Guide?

Show the answer

Description, order and size; the attributes often vary with the domain of work.

R6When is an item ready for selection?

Show the answer

When it can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint.

R7Who sizes the items?

Show the answer

The Developers who will do the work; the Product Owner may help them understand and select trade-offs.

R8What is Product Backlog refinement?

Show the answer

Breaking down and further defining items into smaller, more precise ones; an ongoing activity.

R9List three refinement activities.

Show the answer

Splitting large items, adding detail, sizing, reordering, clarifying with stakeholders, removing obsolete items.

R10Give two reasons for refinement.

Show the answer

Shared understanding; items ready for Planning; better forecasts and confidence; early discovery of risks and dependencies.

R11What is the Product Goal?

Show the answer

A future state of the product that serves as a target to plan against; the Scrum Team's long-term objective; the commitment of the Product Backlog.

R12How many Product Goals at a time?

Show the answer

One; the team fulfils or abandons it before taking on the next.

R13What are the three commitments?

Show the answer

Product Goal (Product Backlog), Sprint Goal (Sprint Backlog), Definition of Done (Increment).

R14What changed from the 2017 Guide?

Show the answer

"Estimate" became "size"; the 10 percent time guideline and "never complete" were removed; the Product Goal and the commitments were added.

9Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Artifacts Product Backlog · Sprint Backlog · Increment; each represents work or value
Commitments Product Goal · Sprint Goal · Definition of Done
Product Backlog Emergent, ordered; the single source of work; the Product Owner is accountable
Items Description, order, size (vary by domain); sized by the Developers
Ready Can be Done within one Sprint
Refinement Breaking down and defining items; ongoing; not an event; as needed, also during the Sprint
Product Goal Future state, long-term objective, in the Product Backlog; one at a time
Product A vehicle to deliver value with a clear boundary, known stakeholders, defined users
Not in the Guide User stories, story points, a refinement time limit
Old wording Estimate, never complete, grooming, 10% (2017)
